summary.text: A continental shelf is the part of a continent that lies under fairly shallow water, a stretch of sea called a shelf sea.
With a few exceptions it ends at the shelf break, at a remarkably uniform depth of roughly 140 m, where the much steeper continental slope begins.
Shelf seas cover only about 8% of the ocean's surface, yet they support 15–20% of the world's primary productivity.

facts.label: Widest shelf
facts.value: Siberian Shelf, up to 1,500 km wide

items.prompt: Little of the sediment covering today's continental shelves came from present-day rivers. When was most of it laid down?

options.label: During the last ice age, when seas were lower
Over the last few centuries, by floods
By recent eruptions of undersea volcanoes
By sea creatures in the last thousand years

items.explain: Some 60–70% of shelf sediment is relict sediment, deposited during the last ice age when sea level was 100–120 m lower.

items.prompt: Off the coast of Chile there is almost no continental shelf at all. What best explains this?

options.label: Strong Pacific waves wash the shelf away
Chile's rivers carry too little sand
An oceanic plate dives beneath the continent there
The water there is too cold for sediment

items.explain: Shelves can be nearly absent where the edge of an oceanic plate plunges beneath continental crust in an offshore subduction zone, as off Chile.

items.prompt: A diver samples the seabed starting near the beach and working far out across the shelf. How does the sediment change along the way?

options.label: From clay near shore to sand farther out
From sand near shore to silt and clay farther out
From sand near shore to boulders farther out
It stays the same coarse sand throughout

items.explain: Sediment usually gets finer with distance from the coast: sand stays in shallow, wave-stirred water, while silt and clay settle in quieter, deeper water offshore.

items.prompt: Why can shallow shelf seas be so rich in life compared with their small share of the ocean?

options.label: Their water never gets cold
Their shallow depth and faster currents mix the water
They have no predators living in them
Their water is completely fresh

items.explain: Shelf seas are often highly productive because shallow water and faster currents cause mixing.

items.prompt: Around most of the world, the shelf ends at about the same depth, roughly 140 m. What is the likely reason?

options.label: It is where sunlight stops reaching
It is where oceanic crust begins
Tides cannot reach any deeper
It marks low sea levels of past ice ages

items.explain: The uniform depth of the shelf break is likely a hallmark of past ice ages, when sea level was lower than now.

items.prompt: In a temperate shelf sea, one spot is shallow with strong tides and no rivers nearby. What happens to its water in summer?

options.label: A warm layer forms over cold deep water
It turns into fresh, brackish water
It stays well mixed from top to bottom
It freezes over from the surface down

items.explain: In shallow water with strong tides and away from river mouths, tidal turbulence beats surface heating, so the water stays well mixed all year.
